**Figure 20.** Episodic coastal-retreat reach. Water-table drawdown contoured inland from the eroding dune-edge front for a single Storm Brendan-scale retreat event (≈6 m at the front, early 2020), over the fitted inland reach (L_cg ≈ 900 m; §4.11). Coastal retreat at this shore is episodic, concentrated in storm events; the per-event edge drawdown is scaled from the chronic gradient through the retreat rate measured over the same period as that gradient (E_c = 2.32 m/yr, 2006--2026, from shoreline positions digitized in this study). The C3 wells fall within the reach while the C2 wells lie largely east of it; the forest boundary and Llyn Rhos-Ddu are marked.

[]{#anchor-14}The clustering (Figures 4 and 5) and the mechanistic coefficients (Figures 12--14 and Table 1) show the same structure. This is consistent with a partition that reflects the aquifer rather than the linkage method. The drainage decay half-life (Table 6; Figure 15) orders the clusters the same way. C1 Lake Edge drains fastest and C4 Main Forest most slowly. C5 is distinct from C4 despite sharing the same canopy.

## []{#anchor-15}5.2 Substrate versus surface control: interpreting the coefficients

[]{#anchor-16}The two forested clusters are inferred to share the deep sandy substrate of the western block, and they carry the same Corsican pine canopy. Yet they segregate into distinct units. Resolving why is central to interpreting what the SSM coefficients measure.

Within the forest zone, elevation alone explains 98% of the variance in atmospheric draw (β₂ versus elevation, r = 0.989). C4 and C5 separate completely on this axis and on mean elevation (10.6 m versus 5.6 m). C4, on the elevated ridge flank, has a deeper water table and unsaturated zone, together with weaker drainage. We interpret this deeper profile as permitting stronger atmospheric draw. C5, on the lower coastal fringe, has a shallower water table and faster drainage. The measured contrast in water-table depth and coefficient behaviour is clear.

That interpretation has independent measured support at this site. Freeman (2008) recorded the water table beneath the Newborough plantation approximately 1.07 m below the open Warren (ANOVA p \< 0.001). She also recorded mean volumetric soil moisture there at roughly half the open-dune value. She attributed the moisture contrast to the loss of capillary contact between the upper soil layers and the water table where the water table is deeper. The forest zone therefore carries an unsaturated zone that is both thicker and drier, consistent with the coefficient contrast we recover.

The substrate explanation differs in confidence between the two clusters. For C4, the bedrock of the ridge outcrops within the forest, so the nature of the rock underlying the cluster is established. Its depth and extent beneath C4 are not known without coring. But the impeded drainage there is consistent with a shallow, irregular bedrock base close beneath the wells, an inference supported by the proximity of the outcropping ridge. The storage evidence within the plantation supports it directly. Across the fourteen forested wells, the specific yield falls with elevation (r = −0.93, p \< 0.001) and rises with distance from the ridge (r = +0.81, p \< 0.001). This is the pattern expected where a shallowing bedrock base thins the drainable sand column toward the outcrop. The relationship is robust to excluding the two anomalous ridge-flank wells (r = +0.79 against ridge distance with both removed). It is present in the uncorrected estimates as well as the corrected ones (r = +0.70, p = 0.005), so it is not an artefact of the canopy correction. For C5, the proposed more-uniform, deeper coastal sand is the weaker inference, resting on the coefficients and topography alone.

On that basis, the split is best read as a substrate-and-topographic-position discontinuity beneath a constant canopy, rather than an arbitrary division of a continuous population. The forest-interception drawdown footprint (Figure 19) occupies the same corner. The high atmospheric draw, the positive water-balance residual and the modelled drawdown reach therefore together describe one coherent forest signature. All three, however, are anchored to the same plantation-and-ridge zone, so their spatial agreement is mutual consistency rather than independent corroboration.

This finding clarifies a potential misreading of the cluster contrasts. The forested clusters carry the highest LCSC values in the network, which might be read as low aquifer drainability. But LCSC is a recharge-sensitivity descriptor, not a storage parameter. The fitted β₁ absorbs canopy interception alongside the true storage response. Part of the forest clusters' elevated LCSC therefore reflects the suppression of throughfall by the canopy, rather than a difference in the aquifer itself.

The water-table-fluctuation specific yields bear on this directly. The uncorrected forest medians exceed the open-dune range. This is because the method attributes the full rainfall total to recharge, when in reality the canopy intercepts roughly a quarter of it. Once corrected for interception, C4's forest median (0.261) falls within the open-dune range (0.210--0.325). C5's (0.330) sits just above its upper edge, though C5's estimate is constrained by the physical-plausibility limit and is only weakly corroborative. The interpolated specific-yield surface shows no discontinuity at the cluster margins.

The effective storage inferred from the water-table response therefore varies smoothly and continuously across the site, stepping nowhere at the cluster margins. This is consistent with, though on these data not proof of, a well-mixed aeolian depositional history. The C4 specific yield and the continuous Sy surface, rather than the ceiling-bound C5 estimate, carry the argument that the forest clusters' distinctive coefficient signature derives largely from a surface boundary condition (canopy interception) rather than from a different subsurface architecture.

A depth-dependent extension of the model lets atmospheric draw decline as the capillary fringe retreats from the root zone with increasing water-table depth. It indicates that a real depth-coupling effect is present at every cluster. The effect is strongest where the water table is shallowest (C1) and weakest where it is deepest (C4). Notably, C4 shows the weakest depth coupling despite carrying the highest atmospheric-draw coefficient. This is consistent with its high β₂ reflecting low specific yield rather than a depth-dependent evapotranspiration pathway. The standard fixed-β₂ model absorbs the coupling as an effective depth-averaged parameter. The depth coupling and the lateral-drainage geometry together contribute to the within-forest β₂ variation, alongside substrate. But the dominant control on the cluster-level contrast remains topographic position and substrate rather than canopy. These within- and cross-cluster comparisons rest on the ordering of β₂ rather than on its absolute magnitude. The fitted β₂ values are OLS estimates biased somewhat high in absolute terms. They are reliable as rankings rather than as quantitative atmospheric-draw rates.

## 5.3 Recharge, loss and the water balance

[]{#recharge-loss-and-the-water-balance}Decomposed under identical climate forcing, the clusters reveal markedly different recharge sensitivities and loss partitions. At the same time, the decomposition closes the monthly water balance to within 1.8% of total losses at every cluster. Recharge declines systematically from the Lake Edge through the open dune to the forested clusters, and total losses track recharge closely. The partition between drainage and atmospheric draw, however, varies sharply. Drainage dominates at C1 (85% of losses at the project datum), reflecting rapid lateral exchange with the lake. Atmospheric draw dominates at C4 (76%). There, the suppressed recharge pulse never lifts the water table far enough above equilibrium to generate a strong drainage response, and the irregular substrate impedes what drainage there is.

The suppression has two components. Interception removes a fraction of rainfall at the crown. In addition, the profile beneath the canopy is measurably drier, so a larger storage deficit must be satisfied before the remainder reaches the water table; Freeman (2008) recorded roughly half the open-dune volumetric soil moisture beneath the plantation. Her felled clearing plot carried a water table statistically indistinguishable from the open Warren. This indicates that the second component is a consequence of the canopy rather than an independent property of the forest zone.

The displacement formulation is what makes this contrast resolvable. Fitted on depth below ground alone, the drainage coefficient is negative at two of the five clusters. From a datum of 1.6 m downward, it is positive and significant at all five (Hollingham, 2026c).

Two cautions attach to the recharge term. First, the model is fitted without an intercept. In an open-boundary system the recharge coefficient can therefore absorb unmeasured boundary fluxes (Young, 2011; Knotters and van Walsum, 1997). β₁·P should not be read as a direct measure of local precipitation reaching the water table. Second, the atmospheric-draw coefficient is an effective parameter. Thornthwaite PET is an energy-based demand index, and it does not define a reference surface in the manner of Penman--Monteith. β₂ therefore folds transpiration, interception, specific yield and depth coupling into a single scaling between atmospheric demand and water-table response, and a formal crop-coefficient decomposition does not apply. Both cautions are consistent with the substrate interpretation above. The coefficients are diagnostic of behaviour. Their physical decomposition requires the independent specific-yield and depth-coupling evidence assembled here.

## 5.4 Boundary conditions and the water-balance residual field

[]{#anchor-17}The near-closure of the water balance at the cluster mean also holds in space. The residual at the wells is modelled losses minus modelled recharge, from the fitted coefficients. It lies within ±0.01 m/month at 65 of the 66 reference wells and carries no gradient across the site. Its cluster medians span −0.007 to +0.001 m/month. A positive residual would mark a location where measured rainfall-driven recharge does not fully account for the observed water level, implying an unmodelled input. No well carries such a residual above +0.02 m/month. The fifteen positive residuals are all below +0.01 m/month, and they are largest in the open dune and at the lake edge (NW3, CEH23, NW6) rather than at the ridge. The largest negative residual falls at the ridge-flank well CEH14. On this evidence, no ridge-derived lateral input is required to close the balance, and the residual field provides no positive support for one.

Two further diagnostics constrain what the record could have detected had such an input been present. Two independent diagnostic tests both returned null results: a cross-correlation lag analysis for distance-dependent transport from the ridge, and a seasonal climatology analysis for unmodelled summer evaporative demand. The cross-correlation null is itself qualified by sampling frequency. Monthly observations are an order of magnitude coarser than the days-to-weeks transit times expected for fracture-flow input from a metamorphic bedrock ridge. A real ridge-derived lag could therefore be invisible at this resolution. The null result bears on what the present record can resolve, not on whether the mechanism is operative.

The seasonal phase of the residual narrows the field further. The residual peaks in winter and early spring at the great majority of wells, and at none in summer. That is inconsistent with any vertical-flux parameterization error: systematically underestimated summer PET, an incomplete canopy-interception correction, or any under-resolved summer evaporative demand. All of these would peak in summer, when those fluxes are active. The phase is consistent instead with either a winter-phased nonlinear recharge mechanism or ridge-derived lateral input arriving during the months of greatest rainfall.

A cluster-stratified version of the same climatology shows mean winter-minus-summer residual contrasts of +8.6 mm in C3 (p\<0.001), +5.4 mm in C4 (p=0.068, marginal) and −0.3 mm in C5 (not significant). The C3 \> C4 \> C5 ordering and the magnitude of the C3 signal together rule out canopy-interception over-estimation as the sole driver of the winter--summer contrast, since the largest signal sits in a cluster with no canopy.

The residual pattern is real and reproducible, but its mechanistic attribution is unresolved. This is the appropriate stance for a lumped-parameter framework. The residual field is a structural diagnostic of where the three-term balance is insufficient. It is not a quantified map of lateral flux, because it also absorbs nonlinear soil-moisture dynamics, coefficient sensitivity and any systematic PET bias.

## []{#anchor-18}5.5 Long-term forcing: coastal retreat and the partition of decline

The network-scale gradient regression isolates a forcing that a climate-only analysis would misattribute. Fitted across the open-dune network, it resolves a coast-edge water-table deepening of roughly 26 mm/yr at 150 m from the shoreline. The deepening declines to zero over an inland reach of about 900 m, and of at most about 1 km under alternative climate covariates.

What that decomposition licenses is the removal of the coastal term, not the recovery of a climate rate. The fitted far-field asymptote is a window statistic rather than a rate: it moves across a range of some 24 mm/yr as the fitting window is varied with the well set held fixed. No clean climate baseline therefore follows from the fit, and none is offered here. An attribution analysis at this site must estimate its own baseline. What it should take from the decomposition is that a spatially structured coastal forcing exists at the western shore, and that this forcing has to be separated first rather than folded into an apparent network-wide decline.

The result is robust to functional form at the network scale and to forest-cover inclusion. It identifies coastal retreat as a spatially structured forcing distinct from climate. The gradient component is carried by the wells within the reach, so it is largest at C5, where coastal retreat accounts for about half of the observed summer-minimum decline. It accounts for most of the smaller decline at C3 (87--102% across delete-one-well refits), half of whose wells lie within the reach. C4 carries 74% of a decline the record does not resolve, C1 a negligible component and C2 none.

A departure of the water table from its mean shrinks to about a third of its size (the e-folding time) in 2.0 months at C1 Lake Edge, 4.1 at C2 Dune, 6.3 at C3 Western Residual, 12.0 at C5 Coastal Forest and 15.6 at C4 Main Forest (median well 5.1 months), measured without a model from the autocorrelation of the deseasonalized level (Hollingham, 2026c). Even the fastest far exceeds the duration of individual storm-driven retreat events. The aquifer therefore functions as a low-pass filter on the shoreline forcing: it smooths discrete event-scale shocks into a chronic gradient. This supports the steady-state Dupuit--Forchheimer regression as the appropriate kinematic form.

The chronic gradient resolved here is the time-averaged expression of a retreat process that, at this shore, is episodic rather than steady (Pye & Blott, 2024). Shoreline loss is concentrated in storm events. The early-2020 Storm Brendan, a discrete retreat of order several metres at the dune front, is a recent example. It is set against a mean of E_c = 2.32 m/yr, measured here from shoreline positions digitized across 2006--2026. That mean is the rate used to scale the gradient, because it spans the period over which the gradient is fitted. Reported rates for this frontage vary with window, extent and method. Pye & Blott (2024) record up to 16.3 m at the southern Twyni Penrhos profile over 2013--2022, about 1.8 m/yr at the most active point. A contemporary account of the 2014--2020 window reports roughly 50 m of loss concentrated in storm events (Forgrave, 2020).

Figure 20 maps the inland drawdown reach implied by a single Brendan-scale event. The steady-state regression averages many such events into the per-year deepening rate. The gradient and the episodic map are therefore two views of the same forcing, not competing estimates. Consistent with this, the coast-to-inland head difference is observed to deepen through the record at −27.8 mm/yr once common-mode climate is removed model-free (Section 4.11). A growing gradient is the temporal signature the steady-state regression predicts, and it distinguishes a migrating boundary from a static offset. On its own, though, it cannot separate erosion from a slowly varying substrate. The cored shore-normal transect (Section 5.7) remains the mechanism-resolving test.

Figure 21 draws the coastal forcing along that reach, largest at the shore and declining to nothing across the \~900 m span. The fitted far-field constant is a window statistic, not a site-wide climate background, and is not drawn as a curve. The same hydraulic diffusivity sets the equilibration time for a boundary perturbation to propagate across this reach, and that time is of order years to decades (Gerla, 2019). The coastal signal therefore registers as a chronic, quasi-steady gradient rather than a response to any single retreat event. A rising sea level, moreover, raises the water table at the coast, and the rise decays inland over a comparable reach. The fitted coast-edge gradient is thus the net of two opposing coastal processes. Sea-level rise of approximately 4 mm/yr (UKCP18 north-Wales near-term central estimate) works against the erosion-driven drawdown. This makes the fitted δ₀ a conservative estimate of the erosion component.

![](Pictures/10000000000005F00000027AB8E82EAA.png){width="16.51cm" height="6.886cm"}**Figure 21. **Conceptual reach of coastal retreat and the far-field term. Long-section from the eroding Caernarfon Bay shoreline inland to 900 m, drawn so that the fitted inland reach L_cg ≈ 900 m (§4.11) falls at the right-hand edge; the dune surface and its slack are illustrative, the vertical scale is exaggerated ×58, and a 100 mm bar is given for reference. The coastal water table (solid) is the fitted coast-edge trend accumulated over a twenty-year horizon, declining linearly to zero at the fitted reach; the undisturbed table (dotted) is the same surface without it. At 150 m, where the headline rate is quoted, the twenty-year accumulation is 528 mm. The curve is drawn in to the shoreline, where the fitted amplitude δ₀ = 31.28 mm/yr gives 626 mm; that value is an extrapolation beyond the nearest well, which sits at 147 m. The fitted far-field constant c_far (−0.3 mm/yr, ≈ −6 mm accumulated over the same horizon) is a window statistic rather than a rate (§4.11) and is not drawn: over this reach coastal retreat is the only identified distance-dependent term. The ghosted wedges at the shore mark the shoreline positions implied by a single 6 m storm event and by five- and twenty-year accumulations of the mean retreat rate. The section is a schematic built from the fitted parameters rather than a modelled water-table surface. Adapted from the technical report (Hollingham, 2026d).

[]{#anchor-19}This forcing also reframes the C5 Coastal Forest anomaly. C5 shows the steepest summer-minimum decline in the network, more than twice that of any other cluster. All clusters share the same climate forcing, so this argues against a purely climatic explanation. The position analysis (Section 5.2) and the coastal-gradient analysis converge on the same explanation. C5 occupies the lowest, most coast-proximal position in the network. There, an inferred thin saturated thickness would amplify the head response to any forcing, and the eroding shoreline lies closest.

Four C5 wells enter the gradient subset. One of them, NW9 (419 m from the coast), shows a decline of −32.7 mm/yr, among the steepest and most significant in the network. At that position the fitted gradient predicts a coastal-retreat deepening of roughly 15 mm/yr under either functional form. Because NW9 is a forested well, it is excluded from the open-dune (forest-free) regression. It therefore functions as an out-of-sample sentinel: its observed decline tests the fitted gradient at a near-coast position without contributing to it. The observed −32.7 mm/yr stands against a fitted coastal contribution of about −15 mm/yr. The residual is consistent with the site-wide decline and with the substrate amplification developed in Section 5.2. This agreement further corroborates the gradient at a near-coast position, complementing the shore-normal transect (Section 4.11).

A single well cannot, however, carry a quantified cluster attribution. The C5 figure should be treated as corroborating the gradient's direction and magnitude, not as an independent estimate. Even so, the substrate, position and gradient evidence converge, and this makes coastal proximity the leading explanation for C5's exceptional trajectory. It does not exclude a contribution from the maturing canopy, which this record cannot separate from the other two. The companion paper develops the management implication. Here the point is characterization: the framework distinguishes a coast-proximal, structurally amplified decline from the climate background. That distinction bears directly on how network-wide summer-minimum trends should be attributed.

One boundary mechanism operates alongside the retreat gradient at the most coast-proximal wells. The discharging foreshore is a tidal boundary, so near-coast water tables couple to a constant-head sea boundary. This buffers their short-term variability and holds their mean toward the shoreline. The tidal coupling and the multi-year shoreline retreat are complementary rather than competing. The former smooths event-scale fluctuation at a fixed boundary position. The latter migrates that boundary landward over years. The C5 decline is read against the slower retreat process. The tidal coupling is noted here as the boundary condition that makes near-coast records intrinsically less climate-legible, not as an alternative explanation for the trend.

The decline observed away from the coast, in the clusters that carry no gradient component or a negligible one (C2 and C1), is a candidate for further mechanistic work. At least two non-exclusive climate drivers are candidates. What the gradient regression cannot supply is the quantity those drivers would be fitted to. The panel absorbs the spatially uniform forcing through the cumulative-water-balance covariate. A constant offset trades off exactly against the trend contribution that covariate carries, so no residual far-field rate is isolated here (Section 4.11). The mechanisms below are accordingly motivated by the decline the network records, not by a fitted background. Climate forcing, separately measured over the station record, is the leading candidate for that decline.

The horizon of the decline is also bounded. Ranwell's levelled 1951--53 readings provide the comparison. Set against them, the open slacks he measured stand today within about a decimetre of their mid-century level once the climate of the two periods is allowed for (−0.09 ± 0.10 m at the six sites beyond the coastal reach, over sixty-six years; Hollingham, 2026d, §5.7.9). The decline this record resolves is therefore an excursion within a near-stationary century, not the visible part of a longer trend.

The deterioration is concentrated in the summer months. This is consistent with rising evaporative demand under the documented post-2013 summer warming (Figure 3), acting through the atmospheric-draw term as elevated potential evapotranspiration. That route is, if anything, understated by the forcing. Thornthwaite carries the heat index in its denominator and constructs it from the same temperatures, so the formula partly cancels its own response to warming. Across the station record, a 7.2% rise in mean annual temperature (0.73 °C between 1931--1960 and 1996--2025) produced a rise of only 3.0% in mean annual PET, an elasticity of 0.42. The evaporative demand implied by the temperature record therefore exceeds the demand the model was forced with.

A reduction in effective recharge is also plausible. One example is a shift in the within-month distribution of rainfall, expressed as a declining recharge sensitivity. The two routes sit differently within the framework. The warming signal enters directly through the model's potential-evapotranspiration forcing. A sub-monthly rainfall redistribution, by contrast, is invisible to a monthly model and would surface only as an apparent decline in recharge sensitivity. The framework makes the network-wide signal visible. On the present analysis, it does not resolve which route dominates, or what share of the observed decline either accounts for. Both are noted as forcings the characterization exposes, not results the paper establishes.

## 5.6 Predictive skill and transferability

[]{#predictive-skill-and-transferability}The practical contribution of the framework rests on the benchmarking result. In one-step diagnostic mode the state-space and traditional linear models are nearly indistinguishable, because each prediction is corrected by the previous observation. The distinction emerges under iterative simulation. There the SSM achieves a median Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.77 against the linear model's 0.42. It returns a positive iterative NSE at all but one of the 66 reference wells, against 55 for the linear model. The explicit head-dependent drainage term captures the storage decay that prevents the cumulative drift to which the linear model is prone.

That iterative skill holds far outside the calibration window. The per-well model was driven by the station record from 1930, with the 2005--2026 coefficients and no refitting. It reproduces the seasonal water-table cycle recorded at three levelled pipes in 1951--53 (Ranwell, 1959), with correlations of 0.74--0.91 and the seasonal range to within a tenth of a metre. Those pipes were read fifty-four years before the fitted record begins (Hollingham, 2026d, §5.7.9).

The spatial pattern of the gain is itself a diagnostic. The largest improvements concentrate in the lake-proximal eastern aquifer, where head-dependent drainage is strongest. The smallest occur in the forest interior, where weak drainage makes the storage term nearly dispensable. The improvement map therefore indicates which parts of the aquifer are governed by head-dependent drainage and which approximate a linear climate response. It is a structural characterization obtained without any invasive measurement.

This is the basis for transferability. The framework requires only three fitted parameters per well, a uniform drainage datum, and monthly rainfall and temperature from a single climate station. It does not require hydraulic-conductivity measurements, aquifer-thickness surfaces or lateral-flow modelling. These are precisely the parameter-sparsity constraints that produced calibration difficulties for an earlier distributed-model effort at this site (Betson et al., 2002).

The displacement formulation is the methodological choice that enables this. It references drainage to a datum below ground rather than to the ground surface. In doing so it captures the head-dependence of the drainage response without calibrating the drainage geometry. It also resolves a positive drainage coefficient even in the low-gradient forest interior. The datum itself is site-specific. The shallowest datum at which the drainage term is identified, and the depth beyond which the drainage flux settles, both follow the site's water-table depths. The datum sweep is therefore repeated at each new site rather than the 3.7 m value being reused (Hollingham, 2026c). With that step, any coastal dune aquifer with a manual dipwell network and a nearby climate station can be parameterized in the same way. The diagnostic syntheses demonstrated here (the t½/ΔNSE/Sy characterization, the coefficient atlas, the residual field) follow directly from that parameterization.

One supplementary step reaches outside this core. Rendering the forest-interception drawdown as a physical reach in metres (Figure 19) requires a hydraulic diffusivity. For this, a single literature conductivity (K ≈ 6 m/day; Betson et al., 2002) and a nominal saturated thickness are assumed, the latter uncertain by a factor of two or more. These enter only that illustrative reach length. The core parameterization, the diagnostic syntheses above and the empirically fitted coastal reach (Figure 20) all remain free of conductivity and thickness inputs. The forest reach is accordingly an order-of-magnitude diagnostic rather than a calibrated prediction.

## 5.7 Framework limitations

[]{#discussion}[]{#framework-limitations}The framework's strengths and its limits are two sides of the same design choice. It fits a lumped mass balance independently at each well and interpolates the results geometrically, so it does not resolve lateral groundwater flow. The interpolated coefficient and head surfaces are aggregators of point responses, not a physical flow model. They cannot represent cluster-to-cluster hydraulic coupling, the lateral redistribution of localized recharge perturbations, or the diffusive response of the aquifer to a change in boundary flux. The affinity analysis and the Darcy field show that the clusters are connected along a continuous downslope drainage pathway. Whether a signal originating in one part of the aquifer propagates to another at magnitudes below the framework's resolution therefore cannot be answered here. That is a question for a calibrated continuous-flow model.

The critical unknowns for such a model are the very quantities the present framework avoids. One is hydraulic conductivity, currently constrained by a single tracer test (6.0 m/day; Betson et al., 2002). The other is aquifer thickness, inferred from a handful of borehole logs across the site. A measured K would also tighten the only K-conditioned output of the present framework, the forest-drawdown reach length in Figure 19. As noted in Section 5.6, however, all other framework outputs (SSM coefficients, WTF specific yields, substrate-gradient interpretation, coastal-retreat regression and residual field) are K-independent and would not change with a measured K. The priority field measurements to enable a flow model are slug tests at representative wells per cluster and a ground-penetrating-radar survey of aquifer thickness. These would also support an independent vadose-zone test of the canopy-driven recharge-suppression signal.

The same campaign would test the structural interpretation of the C3 transition (Section 5.1). A south-west to north-east transect would resolve the depth to the estuarine-clay base, carrying the Caernarfon Bay coastal-retreat rate as a covariate. It would establish whether the eastward-to-south-westward buffering gradient reflects a single dipping clay base (one thickening sand column) rather than two distinct substrate blocks. It would also separate that structural control from the confounded coastal and plantation-margin influences.

Several further limitations qualify specific results. The monthly measurement resolution cannot isolate individual storm events. The water-table-fluctuation specific yields therefore conflate gravity drainage with capillary-fringe release, and are upper bounds rather than point estimates (Healy and Cook, 2002; Scanlon et al., 2002). Thornthwaite PET is a temperature-and-daylength index whose absolute magnitude is uncertain. The framework's internal consistency does not depend on it, but absolute flux estimates derived from it do.

The coastal-retreat regression is a steady-state spatial model. It resolves the first-order distance gradient but not the multi-year transient over which an erosion signal propagates inland. Direct measurement of present-day retreat rates at the south-western dune front remains a monitoring priority. The water-balance residual shows no spatial structure at the wells, but its monthly series carries a reproducible winter-phased seasonal pattern. As discussed, the attribution of that pattern between a genuine lateral flux and a modelling artefact is unresolved.

The clusters describe the modern record. Grouped on their 1989--96 readings, the CCW wells did not reproduce them (Section 4.3). The difference lies with the warren wells near the sea: then they moved with the inland warren; today they move with wells on their landward side, near the forest edge. That could mean the ground changed between the two periods, or it could reflect a short early record with many readings at the bottom of the pipe, and the record cannot say which. The clusters are therefore not applied to 1989--96, and gaps are filled from cluster-mates only within the modern record, where the method was tested.

Finally, the water table follows the ground closely only once the DEM is smoothed to the scale of the dune ridges (r = 0.92 at 300 m, against 0.76 at native resolution). Topography is therefore a proxy for the regional form of the water table, co-determined with it by the underlying till and bedrock architecture. It is not a proxy for local flow paths, and DEM-derived surface routing is not a guide to groundwater flow direction.

# 6. Conclusions

This study sets out a parameter-sparse state-space framework for characterizing the hydrogeological architecture of a coastal dune aquifer from routine monitoring data. It demonstrates the framework across 88 dipwells and 21 years of monthly records at Newborough Warren. The principal conclusions are:

1.  **Five hydrogeological clusters govern site hydrology. **The Pearson affinity audit of hydrograph similarity independently supports cluster assignment for 91% (60 of 66) of reference-network wells (Section 4.3). The cluster-level contrasts in SSM coefficients, drainage half-life and specific yield provide mechanistic substantiation. The five units resolve as a responsive eastern block (C1 Lake Edge, C2 Dune), a buffered Western Residual (C3), and two forested clusters distinguished by topographic position and inferred substrate. C4 Main Forest, on the elevated ridge flank, has high atmospheric draw and weak drainage. C5 Coastal Forest lies on the lower coastal ground. Within the forest zone, elevation alone explains 98% of the variance in atmospheric draw, which identifies position and elevation, rather than canopy, as the dominant within-forest control.
2.  **Within the modern record, a well's cluster-mates are a better guide to its missing months than the climate model.** The nearest cluster-mate put back hidden spring levels with a median miss of 0.041 m, against 0.139 m for the SSM on climate alone, including in 2006--08, when the water table stood higher than the climate explains. The clusters are not shown to have held in 1989--96: grouped on their readings then, the 12 CCW wells matched today's clusters no better than chance (adjusted Rand index 0.03). They are not carried back to that period (Section 4.3).
3.  **The aquifer's storage varies smoothly, without discontinuity at the cluster margins; the cluster contrasts are surface-mediated.** Once corrected for canopy interception, the C4 forest specific yield falls within the open-dune range. The interpolated specific-yield surface shows no discontinuity at the cluster margins. The C5 estimate sits at the upper edge of that range and is the least reliable in the network, so it is treated as weakly corroborative. The forest clusters' distinctive coefficient signature therefore derives largely from a surface boundary condition, canopy interception suppressing recharge, rather than from a different subsurface architecture.
4.  **The displacement-formulation SSM closes the water balance and substantially improves forecast skill.** The three-term model closes the monthly water balance to within 1.8% of total losses at every cluster. This is a property of the fit rather than independent evidence, and the split between drainage and evapotranspiration depends on the datum. The model achieves a median iterative Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.77 against 0.42 for a traditional linear model, with a positive iterative NSE at 65 of 66 wells against 55 of 66. The spatial pattern of the improvement is itself a non-invasive diagnostic of where head-dependent drainage governs the aquifer.
5.  **The water balance closes on average and its residual shows no spatial structure at the wells.** Residuals lie within ±0.01 m/month at 65 of the 66 reference wells and carry no gradient across the site. No well exceeds +0.02 m/month, and the largest positive residuals fall in the open dune and at the lake edge rather than in the forest. No unmodelled lateral flux is required to close the balance at any cluster. A cross-correlation lag test and a seasonal climatology test on the monthly residual likewise return null results for ridge-derived input. The monthly sampling interval is, however, coarse relative to the transit times expected of fracture flow, so the nulls bound what this record can resolve rather than excluding the mechanism. The residual field is a structural diagnostic of model adequacy, not a quantified flux map.
6.  **Coastal retreat is a distinct, spatially structured forcing on long-term water-table trends.** A network-scale gradient regression resolves a coast-edge deepening of roughly 26 mm/yr at 150 m from the shoreline, declining over an inland reach of order 1 km. This deepening accounts for about half of the observed summer-minimum decline at the coast-proximal C5 cluster. It also accounts for most of the smaller decline at the Western Residual, half of whose wells lie within the reach. The gradient is corroborated by the progressive deepening of the coast-to-inland head difference along a shore-normal transect. It is spatially structured, strongest at the shore and decaying to nothing over that reach, rather than a uniform decline. The exceptional decline of the coast-proximal C5 cluster is consistent with its coastal position and thin saturated thickness. A contribution from its maturing canopy is not excluded and is left open. Distinguishing this coastal forcing from the climate background is necessary for any correct attribution of network-wide summer-minimum trends.
7.  **The framework is transferable.** It characterizes aquifer architecture (storage, recharge sensitivity, storage decay and flow structure) from manual dipwell records and a single climate station. It does so without coring, hydraulic testing or calibrated continuous-flow modelling. Its one site-specific modelling choice, the drainage datum, is set by repeating the datum sweep of Hollingham (2026c) at each site. Its principal limitation is the converse of this strength. As a geometric aggregator of point responses, it cannot resolve cluster-to-cluster hydraulic coupling. That would need a calibrated flow model, and the hydraulic-conductivity and aquifer-thickness measurements it requires.

[]{#conclusions}The companion paper (Hollingham, 2026b) quantifies the hydrological consequences of the dune-scraping and plantation-clearfell interventions undertaken at the site, within a before-after-control-impact framework.

# Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the manuscript preparation process

During the preparation of this work the author used Anthropic's Claude (successive Claude Opus and Claude Fable models, accessed through the Claude desktop application) for substantial drafting and editing of the manuscript text: composing prose from the author's analytical outputs and decisions, structuring and restructuring sections, and correcting the text against the study's committed analytical outputs. The conception and design of the study, the twenty-one-year manual dipwell record on which it rests, the analytical decisions, and the interpretation of the results are the author's own. Numerical values in the manuscript were verified against the committed outputs of the analysis pipeline, and a decision log records the methodological and editorial calls made by the author during the work. After using this tool the author reviewed and edited the content as needed and takes full responsibility for the content of the published article.
